One second before a behavior, the body is already doing work. It is reading a face, marking a threat, calling up a trained response, and narrowing or widening the next move. Call the habit behavioral time-slicing: you take one visible act and ask what made it more likely at each time depth.

Wilder learns this after a job lead slips away in his inbox. He wants to call himself careless and be done with it. Samantha asks what happened. The message arrived during a crowded handoff. Pull the person back, lock the door, call for help, or say the blunt sentence. The layered account belongs after safety is held. Analysis should make action smarter, not slower when danger is still unfolding.

### Example 3: Kenya Field Admission
